title: The Breaker Box

post.author: u/caretaker_hildegund
post.title: I'm the caretaker of an old apartment block. Last night the front door refused 14 fob taps in under five minutes, because strangers were drying their duvets.

blocks.text: I'm Hildegund, caretaker at Hollinsbury Court. In a cupboard by the boiler sits one small computer that runs the building. Other machines send it questions, such as "may this fob open the door?", and it answers. Each question is a request. A computer that answers requests is called a server.

It answers three things: the front door's fob reader (a fob is the key tag residents tap), the lift buttons, and the basement laundry. Inside the server are 10 helpers. Each takes one request, finishes it, then takes the next. Programmers call a helper a thread, and the set of them a pool.

When all 10 are busy, new requests wait in one line, first come first served. A fob check is 50 ms of work (ms means thousandths of a second). The door reader waits 5 seconds for an answer, then gives up and shows "timed out". A limit like that on waiting is called a timeout.

Paying for a dryer is slower. A helper asks the payment company, Tillpenny, over the internet, and waits for its answer, up to 60 seconds (60 s). If a payment fails, the dryer asks again at once, five tries in all, then shows "payment failed". Asking again after a failure is called a retry. Juozas, who set the server up, keeps its settings in a short text file, in a format called YAML. Each line is a name, its value and a note:

shared_helpers: 10     # doors, lifts, laundry
payment_timeout: 60s   # waiting for Tillpenny
dryer_tries: 5         # then payment failed
fob_wait: 5s           # set in the door reader

Electricity is cheap from 23:00, so the laundry fills then. Last night ten residents were waiting with full baskets. From 23:00:00 they started their dryers one after another, one every 6 seconds. Two more came down, at 23:01:02 and 23:02:30.

Tillpenny was broken in a new way. It accepted every request and never answered. Each payment held its helper for the full minute, failed, and its dryer asked again. By 23:00:54 all 10 helpers were waiting on Tillpenny, and the late dryers queued behind them.

At that hour the front door gets about three taps a minute. From 23:01, each tap joined the line behind payments. Here is the door log, first and last lines; each shows the time, the flat and the result:

23:01:14  flat 9   timed out
23:01:34  flat 22  timed out
23:05:34  flat 31  timed out

Fourteen refusals, from 23:01:14 to 23:05:34. I checked every fob against the laundry list. Not one belongs to a resident with a dryer card. Meanwhile the laundry log showed 10 dryers "waiting for payment" at once, one on every helper.
The front door would not open, because strangers were drying duvets.
Tillpenny has broken before. Every other time it answered at once with an error. The helper was free again within milliseconds, the dryers just said "payment failed", and nobody's door ever stuck.
Agnieszka in flat 22 stood in the rain until I let her in with my master key. What should Juozas change before the next cheap-rate night?

The front door answers taps until 23:01:09; from 23:01:14 to 23:05:34 it refuses 14 taps. The dryers wait for payment from 23:00:00 and fail one by one from 23:05:30.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your boiler room has a fuse box. When one flat's kettle shorts, that flat's breaker trips and cuts just that circuit, so one bad kettle can't burn the house down or black out the stairs. Software borrowed the idea and called it a circuit breaker. It counts failed calls to one outside service. After so many failures in a short time it trips, and for a while it answers "failed" at once, without calling. Then it lets one call through as a test. So, questions. What was in the line ahead of each refused fob? How long does a helper spend on a fob, and how long did it spend on a payment last night? And what did the helpers do on the nights Tillpenny said no at once?

replies.author: u/caretaker_hildegund
replies.text: Ahead of every refused fob were payments: the late dryers', and the ones asking again. A fob takes 50 ms; a payment took the full 60 s last night. On the error nights the helpers were free again at once. One more thing: Tillpenny is only how residents pay on the spot. Every flat already pays the building a monthly service charge, and I can add anything to it.

comments.author: u/more_threads_mehmetcan
comments.text: You just need more threads. Ten is tiny; your phone is running hundreds right now. A helper that is only waiting costs almost nothing, because it isn't working. Set shared_helpers to 20 and there are always spare ones for the door, however many dryers are stuck. A breaker only makes payments fail faster; the door's problem is too few threads. Bigger pool, no line, problem gone.

comments.author: u/shorter_wait_kristof
comments.text: A 60 second wait for a card payment is mad. The supermarket's answers in two. Set payment_timeout to 10s and each stuck payment lets go of its helper six times sooner. And have the server retry a failed payment a couple of times before telling the dryer, so a payment that fails once gets another chance and fewer duvets stay wet.

reply.prompt: Cheap-rate nights come every night, and Tillpenny could hang again on any of them. What should Juozas change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Raise the shared pool from 10 helpers to 20, so the dryers can never take up all of them.
options.verdict: Twenty fill too, a little later
options.part2: Juozas set shared_helpers to 20. We replayed last night in the sim: 12 dryers held 12 helpers, 8 stayed free, and the door refused nobody. Every dryer still said "payment failed" after five minutes of waiting. Then in January Tillpenny hung on a Sunday when all 24 dryers ran, started between 23:00:00 and 23:02:50. By 23:00:57 all 20 helpers were waiting on it, and the door refused 13 taps between 23:01:14 and 23:05:34. Twenty filled, just a little later than ten.
options.senior: A bigger shared pool only moves the moment it fills. While anything that waits on an outside service shares helpers with everything else, a hang will sooner or later hold them all: more dryers, a slower answer or a longer outage. Waiting helpers aren't free either; each holds memory and an open connection. The fix is to stop one service's waiting from reaching the shared helpers at all.

options.text: Cut the payment timeout from 60 s to 10 s, so a stuck payment lets go of its helper sooner.
options.part2: Juozas set payment_timeout to 10s. In the sim's replay of last night the door refused nobody: each dryer held one helper 10 s at a time, and never more than 9 were busy at once. But every dryer still waited 50 s through five tries and said "payment failed", so nobody dried anything. Then in January Tillpenny hung on a Sunday when all 24 dryers ran. The 10 helpers filled at 23:00:27, and the door refused 2 taps, at 23:00:54 and 23:01:14.
options.senior: A shorter timeout is the cheapest real improvement and usually right: wait about as long as a healthy answer takes at its slowest, not a minute. But it only shortens each hold. A dozen slow calls can still take the shared helpers together, and the dryers still get nothing. It belongs in the fix, alongside a separate pool and a breaker.

options.text: Have the server retry each failed payment twice, so fewer dryers end up saying payment failed.
options.part2: Juozas made the server retry each failed payment twice before telling the dryer. Against a company that never answers, every try waited the full 60 s, so each payment held its helper for three minutes, and each dryer still asked five times. In the sim's replay the door refused 51 taps, from 23:01:14 to 23:17:54. Not one dryer was paid.
options.senior: Retries help when failures are brief and random, and only for calls that are safe to repeat. Against a service that hangs, each retry is another full timeout of waiting, on top of the caller's own retries: here 3 server tries for each of 5 dryer tries, 15 waits per dryer. Retrying piles more load onto the one thing that is already failing.

options.text: Give payments their own 2 helpers behind a breaker, and answer pay later when they fail.
options.part2: Juozas split the pool: 8 helpers for the doors, lifts and laundry, and 2 for Tillpenny only. A healthy payment takes about a second, so he let each wait at most 3 s. In front of the 2 he put a breaker. After 5 failed payments within 60 s it trips, and for 30 s it answers "pay later, added to your service charge" at once. Then it lets one payment through as a test. In the sim's replay, dryers 1 to 5 waited 3 s each, then ran on pay later. The breaker tripped at 23:00:27, and dryers 6 to 10 got pay later at once. The tests at 23:01:02 and 23:02:30 failed, so it stayed open. None of the 8 helpers ever waited on Tillpenny, and the door refused nobody. When Tillpenny answers a test again, the breaker closes. All 12 duvets dried, and the charges went on the next bill.
options.senior: Fence each outside service into its own small pool, a bulkhead, so its waiting can only use up its own helpers. Give it a timeout near a healthy answer's slowest. Put a breaker in front, so a dead service is failed fast instead of waited on, and is tested with one call to see if it is back. Then decide what a failure should say. Here pay later is a safe fallback, because the residents are known and billed every month anyway.

sim.title: Run cheap-rate night at Hollinsbury Court
sim.lede: You're Juozas, replaying last night from 23:00:00, one second per tick. 10 shared helpers. Ten dryers start one every 6 s from 23:00:00, and two more at 23:01:02 and 23:02:30. Each payment asks Tillpenny and waits up to the payment timeout, 60 s; after a failure the dryer asks again at once, 5 tries in all. The front door gets a fob tap every 20 s, at :09, :29 and :49 past each minute, and the reader gives up after 5 s in line. Pick the pool, the payment timeout, server retries, separate helpers for payments, a breaker and pay later, and how Tillpenny behaves. Then run the night. The breaker trips after 5 failed payments within 60 s, answers at once for 30 s, then lets one payment through as a test.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run as built. All 10 helpers are busy from 23:00:54, and the door refuses 14 taps, 23:01:14 to 23:05:34. Set Tillpenny to errors at once and start the night again: nobody is refused. Now try each reply. 20 helpers: 0 refused tonight, then 13 with 24 dryers. A 10 s timeout: 0 tonight, 2 with 24 dryers, and no dryer paid. Two server retries: 51 refused. Own 2 helpers, a 3 s timeout, a breaker and pay later: 0 refused, 12 on pay later. Last, run that to 23:03:10, set Tillpenny to answer and start one more dryer: its payment is the test, and the breaker closes.

explain.oneLine: Nothing was wrong with the door. Tillpenny hung instead of failing, every payment held its helper for the full 60 s, and the dryers kept asking again, so the one shared pool was full of waiting from 23:00:54. Fob checks, which need 50 ms, queued behind payments and gave up after 5 s: 14 times. One outside service had no fence around it, and nothing stopped the calls once it was clearly down.

steps.title: Ten helpers, all waiting on one company.
steps.text: Here is what each payment did. First a dryer's request reached the front of the line, and a free helper took it. Then the helper sent it to Tillpenny and waited. Tillpenny accepted it and never answered, so the helper waited the full 60 s timeout. Then it reported a failure, and the dryer asked again at once. What went wrong: the ten dryers started one every 6 s, so by 23:00:54 each of the 10 helpers held one payment. Every time a helper came free, another payment was waiting for it, from a late dryer or a dryer asking again. Twelve dryers, five tries each, a minute per try: about six minutes of 10 helpers doing nothing but waiting.

steps.title: Why a fob waited behind strangers' laundry.
steps.text: The line is first come first served, and it does not care what kind of request is in it. A fob tap at 23:01:09 joined the line behind payments that were already waiting. A helper comes free only when a payment times out, and the next payments in line took the first ones. The reader gave up at 23:01:14, 5 s after the tap. The same happened to every tap from 23:01:09 to 23:05:29, three a minute: 14 refusals. A 50 ms job was stuck behind 60 s jobs that shared its helpers; quick work waiting behind slow work in one line is called head-of-line blocking. That is the same shape as one slow channel holding up the rest (s4e10), and as a pool used up by long waits (s3e01).

steps.title: A hang is worse than an error.
steps.text: On earlier nights Tillpenny failed by saying no at once. The helper got the error within milliseconds and was free again; the dryer's five tries took a moment and it showed "payment failed". Nobody noticed at the door. Last night it accepted requests and said nothing, which uses up the caller's waiting instead of its work. The timeout decides how long each hang costs: 60 s here. Many systems are tested against errors and never against silence.

steps.title: A breaker, step by step.
steps.text: A circuit breaker sits in front of calls to one service and has three states. Closed: calls go through, and it counts the failures. If 5 fail within 60 s, it trips to open. Open: every call fails at once, without using a helper or waiting, for 30 s. Then it goes half-open: it lets one call through as a test. If the test is answered, it closes; if it fails, it opens for another 30 s. What can go wrong: a threshold too low trips on ordinary blips, one too high waits through many timeouts first, and a test that keeps failing means callers need a fallback, not just a fast "no".

steps.title: Bulkheads and fallbacks.
steps.text: A ship is split into compartments by walls called bulkheads, so one hole floods one compartment, not the ship. In software a bulkhead is a separate small pool for each outside service. Here, 2 helpers for Tillpenny and 8 for everything else. If the 2 are busy, a payment fails at once instead of joining the shared line. A fallback is what you answer when the real answer can't come. Here it is "pay later, added to your service charge": a safe lie, because every resident is known and billed each month. What can go wrong: a fallback that says something false that matters (a card check that lets everyone in) is not safe; there, failing closed and calling a person is the answer.

diagram.aria: The fix. Fob checks from the front door and lifts go to 8 shared helpers that never wait on Tillpenny. The 12 dryers' payments go through a breaker that trips after 5 failures in 60 s. While it is closed, payments go to 2 payment helpers with a 3 s limit, which call Tillpenny. While it is open, payments get the fallback: pay later, added to the service charge.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next cheap-rate night. The door's fob checks have 8 helpers that never wait on Tillpenny. Payments go through a breaker to their own 2 helpers with a 3 s limit; once 5 have failed within 60 s the breaker answers pay later at once. In the sim: 0 refusals and 12 dryers on pay later.

fix.title: The fix: fence the payments off, fail them fast, and say pay later
fix.text: Split the pool: shared_helpers: 8 for the doors, lifts and laundry screens, and payment_helpers: 2 for Tillpenny only, with no line of their own, so a payment that finds both busy fails at once. Set payment_timeout: 3s, well above a healthy answer's slowest (about a second at Hollinsbury) and far below a minute. Put a breaker on the payment calls: trip after 5 failures within 60 s, stay open 30 s, then one test call. Make every failure answer "pay later, added to your service charge", and log each one so the charges reach the next bill. Add a check that would have caught this: busy helpers per pool, and the breaker's state, on the caretaker's screen. In the sim: 0 refusals, 12 dryers on pay later, and the breaker closing the moment Tillpenny answers a test.

limits: Pay later is only safe because the residents are known and billed monthly. A fallback that answers something false where it matters, such as a door check that lets everyone in while the server is down, is not safe; there the fallback should fail closed and call a person.

The thresholds are guesses until measured. Five failures in 60 s and 30 s open suit a dozen dryers a night; a busy service needs a failure rate over a larger window, or a breaker trips on a normal bad minute or waits too long on a real outage.

A bulkhead fences waiting, not everything. The 2 payment helpers still share the server's memory and network with the rest, and a breaker only protects the calls that go through it: the next outside service (a lift company, a parcel locker) needs its own.

explain.seniorTake: A call to something you don't control will, sooner or later, usually hang rather than fail at least once, and a hang spends your capacity, not theirs. So give each outside service its own small pool, a bulkhead, sized for its normal load, and a timeout near a healthy answer's slowest. Put a breaker in front so a service that is clearly down is failed fast and then tested with one call, instead of waited on by every request. Decide, per call, what a failure should say: a safe fallback where being wrong for a while costs little and can be put right later, and an honest error where it can't. Retries and bigger pools are not fixes for a hang; they multiply the waiting. A later case, Field Report: The Breaker at Scale, looks at Hystrix, one company's breakers.

realWorld.title: Martin Fowler, 2014: the circuit breaker pattern
realWorld.text: Fowler writes that "remote calls can fail, or hang without a response until some timeout limit is reached", and that with many callers "you can run out of critical resources leading to cascading failures across multiple systems." His fix: "You wrap a protected function call in a circuit breaker object, which monitors for failures. Once the failures reach a certain threshold, the circuit breaker trips". In the half-open state "the circuit is ready to make a real call as trial to see if the problem is fixed." Fowler credits the pattern to Nygard: "Michael Nygard popularized the Circuit Breaker pattern to prevent this kind of catastrophic cascade."

realWorld.title: Michael Nygard, Release It! (2nd edition, 2018)
realWorld.text: Nygard's Release It!, second edition (Pragmatic Bookshelf, January 2018) lists "Circuit Breaker" and "Bulkheads" in its Stability Patterns chapter, and "Integration Points" and "Cascading Failures" among its stability antipatterns.

realWorld.title: Resilience4j: three states
realWorld.text: Resilience4j, a Java library, says its CircuitBreaker "is implemented via a finite state machine with three normal states: CLOSED, OPEN and HALF_OPEN". It changes from CLOSED to OPEN "when the failure rate is equal or greater than a configurable threshold", or when the share of slow calls is. It "rejects calls with a CallNotPermittedException when it is OPEN", and "After a wait time duration has elapsed" it goes HALF_OPEN and "permits a configurable number of calls to see if the backend is still unavailable or has become available again."

realWorld.title: Resilience4j: the defaults
realWorld.text: Its documented defaults: a failure rate threshold of 50%, a sliding window of the last 100 calls, at least 100 calls before it judges, 10 calls let through when half-open, and 60,000 ms in the open state. A call counts as slow after 60,000 ms by default: the same minute Tillpenny's helpers waited. Hollinsbury's 5 failures in 60 s are a small building's numbers, not these.

realWorld.title: Resilience4j: bulkheads
realWorld.text: "Resilience4j provides two implementations of a bulkhead pattern that can be used to limit the number of concurrent execution": a SemaphoreBulkhead, and "a FixedThreadPoolBulkhead which uses a bounded queue and a fixed thread pool." The semaphore kind allows 25 calls at once by default, and its maxWaitDuration defaults to 0: a call that finds it full is refused at once, like Hollinsbury's 2 payment helpers.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 availability, criterion A1.1
realWorld.text: A1.1 expects the company to maintain, monitor and evaluate current processing capacity and use of system components. A pool one partner can fill is exactly that kind of capacity.

asked: What are a circuit breaker's three states?
interview.answer: A circuit breaker wraps calls to one dependency. Closed, calls pass and it counts failures, usually as a failure rate over a sliding window of recent calls, often counting slow calls too. When the rate crosses a threshold it opens: calls fail immediately without touching the dependency, so callers don't spend threads and time waiting on something that's down. After a wait it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through; if they succeed it closes, if not it opens again. A bulkhead isolates resources per dependency, typically a small thread pool or a concurrency limit, so one slow dependency can only exhaust its own share and not the pool that serves everything else. You size it from normal load and give it little or no queue, so overflow fails fast. A fallback is what you return when the real call fails or the breaker is open. It's safe when being wrong for a while is cheap and can be corrected later, such as a cached value, a default, or deferring a charge to a known, billed customer. It's unsafe when the answer gates something that matters, such as access or safety, where you should fail closed and alert a person. A story I'd tell: an apartment block's server ran door fobs and dryer payments on one pool of 10 threads. The payment provider started accepting connections and never replying, with a 60 s timeout, and dryers retried. All 10 threads were waiting from 23:00:54, and 14 door taps timed out behind them. The fix was 2 threads just for payments with a 3 s timeout, a breaker in front, and "pay later" as the fallback: no refusals, every dryer ran.

terms.def: The old apartment block in this story. One small server in a cupboard by the boiler runs its front door, lifts and basement laundry.
The person who looks after a building day to day: repairs, keys, bins, and letting people in. Hildegund is Hollinsbury's.
A small key tag a resident taps on a reader to open the door. The reader asks the server whether that fob may open it.
The pad by the front door that reads a fob and asks the server. It waits 5 s for an answer, then shows "timed out".
One question one machine sends another and waits to have answered, such as "may this fob open the door?" or "take this dryer payment".
A computer whose job is to answer other machines' requests. Hollinsbury's is one small box by the boiler.
One worker inside the server that takes one request at a time, finishes it, then takes the next, like one clerk at a counter. Programmers call it a thread (s1e08).
A fixed set of helpers shared by every request, like a row of clerks serving one queue. Hollinsbury's shared pool had 10. A pool can be used up when every helper is busy (s3e01).
Where requests wait for a free helper, first come first served. It does not care whether a request takes 50 ms or 60 s.
Short for millisecond: a thousandth of a second. A fob check takes 50 ms, a twentieth of a second.
A limit on how long to wait for an answer before giving up. The fob reader's is 5 s; the payment's was 60 s.
Asking again after a failure. Each dryer asked again at once, five tries in all, before showing "payment failed".
The outside payment company the dryers use. Its computer is reached over the internet; tonight it accepted every request and never answered.
A business that takes card payments on behalf of others, like the card machine at a shop. The dryers pay through Tillpenny.
When a service takes a request and never answers, so the caller waits until its timeout. Worse than an error, which frees the caller at once.
A fast "no" from a service. On Tillpenny's earlier outages each payment got one within milliseconds, so the helper was free again straight away.
A resident's card for the basement laundry. None of the 14 refused fobs belonged to a resident with one.
What each flat pays the building every month for upkeep. The caretaker can add costs to it, which is what makes "pay later" safe here.
A tariff where power costs less at night, at Hollinsbury from 23:00, so many residents start their dryers then.
A short text file of names and values that tells a program how to behave, such as shared_helpers: 10. A # starts a note that the program ignores.
The setting for the size of the shared pool: 10 as built, 8 after the fix.
The setting for how long a helper waits for Tillpenny: 60 s as built, 3 s after the fix.
The setting the fix adds: how many helpers serve Tillpenny payments only. 2, with no line of their own.
A plain text format for settings: one name per line, a colon, then its value. Juozas's settings file is written in it.
How many times a dryer asks to pay before showing "payment failed": 5.
When quick jobs wait in a line behind slow ones, so the slow ones decide how long everyone waits. The fobs waited behind payments.
The box of switches that protects a building's wiring. Each circuit has a breaker that cuts it when something on it shorts.
A guard in front of calls to one service. After too many failures it trips and fails calls at once for a while, then tests with one call, like a fuse box breaker.
The normal state: calls go through, and the breaker counts the failures.
The tripped state: every call fails at once without being sent, for a set time. Hollinsbury's stays open 30 s.
After the open spell, the breaker lets one call through as a test. Answered, it closes; failed, it opens again.
A breaker switching from closed to open, here after 5 failed payments within 60 s.
The one call a half-open breaker lets through to see whether the service is back.
Giving a caller an immediate "no" instead of making it wait for a timeout, so the helper is free again at once.
The most recent stretch a breaker counts over, such as the last 60 s or the last 100 calls, moving forward as time passes.
The share of failed calls in the window at which a breaker trips. Resilience4j's default is 50%.
A call that took longer than a set time. Resilience4j can trip on too many slow calls as well as failed ones.
A wall that splits a ship into compartments so one leak floods one part. In software, a separate small pool or limit for each outside service.
The answer given when the real one can't come, such as "pay later, added to your service charge". Safe only when being wrong for a while is cheap and can be put right.
When a check can't be made, refuse rather than allow. Right for a door check; wrong for a dryer payment.
One part failing and taking others down with it, here a payment company's hang stopping the front door.
A free Java library of protection patterns for calls to other services: circuit breakers, bulkheads, retries, rate limiters and timeouts.
A common programming language. Resilience4j is written for it.
The error Resilience4j's breaker gives a caller at once while it is open, instead of making the call.
Resilience4j's bulkhead that counts calls in progress and refuses any over its limit, 25 by default.
Resilience4j's bulkhead that runs calls on its own fixed pool of threads with a bounded line.
How long a call may wait to enter a full Resilience4j bulkhead. The default, 0, refuses it at once.
Nygard's name for any place a system calls another system. Every one can fail or hang.
A test that breaks something on purpose, such as making one backend slow, to check the protections react as designed.
A service that a front program passes requests on to. In Build Night G6, the servers behind Gatekeeper.
The reverse proxy you build across Build Nights. G6 adds timeouts, retries, a circuit breaker per backend and rate limiting.
A hands-on project session that unlocks after certain cases. G6 unlocks after Wait Longer, The Breaker Box and The Bouncer.
Short for application programming interface: the agreed way one program asks another for something, such as a partner's payment service.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria.
A SOC 2 availability criterion: the company maintains, monitors and evaluates current processing capacity and use of system components.

atWork: Look for one slow partner API that shares a thread or connection pool with pages that never call it. It is a common pattern: a payment, shipping or address-lookup call with a generous timeout sits in the same pool as everything else, until the partner hangs instead of failing and unrelated pages start timing out. Check three things for each outside call. Does it share a pool with anything else? How long may it wait, against how long it takes when healthy? And what should it answer when the partner is down: a safe fallback, or an honest error? Build Night G6 (Gatekeeper; unlocks after Wait Longer, this case and The Bouncer) has you add a circuit breaker per backend and a chaos test with one slow backend that shows the breaker opening, half-opening and closing. Standards: if your company is pursuing SOC 2's availability criteria, A1.1 expects it to maintain, monitor and evaluate current processing capacity and use of system components. A pool one partner can fill is a capacity risk, so chart busy threads per pool and breaker state, and alert on them now rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's web shop runs on one server with a pool of 50 worker threads. Product pages, the basket and checkout share them. Checkout calls an outside fraud-check service with a 30 s timeout. One evening the fraud service starts accepting connections and never replying, and within two minutes product pages time out too, though they never call it. What is happening, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Checkout calls waiting on the hung service hold every shared thread, so unrelated pages queue behind them
Give the fraud check its own small pool, a bulkhead, so it can only use up its own threads
A shorter timeout and a circuit breaker that fails fast while the service is down, with a fallback answer

recall.model: The fraud service hangs instead of failing, so every checkout call holds a thread for the full 30 s. Checkouts keep coming, the shared pool is full of threads stuck waiting, and product pages queue behind them and time out though they never call the service: one dependency has used up all the threads. I'd give the fraud check its own small pool, a bulkhead, sized for normal checkout traffic with little or no queue, so it can only use up its own threads. I'd set a shorter timeout near a healthy answer's slowest, and put a circuit breaker in front that trips after a run of failures, fails fast while open, and tests with one call. Then a fallback: for example accept low-value orders and check them later, and hold large ones for a person.

recall.prompt: A circuit breaker on calls to a payment service has just tripped. What does it do with the next call while it is open?
options: Sends it and waits the full timeout
Fails it at once without calling the service
Holds it in a line until the service answers
Sends it to the service twice, then gives up
recall.why: Open means the breaker has decided the service is down, so it answers at once without sending the call. No helper waits. At Hollinsbury the dryers got pay later at once from 23:00:27, while the breaker was open.

recall.prompt: After its open spell, a breaker goes half-open. What does it do then?
options: Closes, and sends every call that came in meanwhile
Lets one test call through, and closes or opens again by its result
Stays open until someone resets it by hand
Sends calls to a second copy of the service
recall.why: Half-open is a careful check: one call (or a few) goes through. Answered, the breaker closes; failed, it opens again for another spell. At Hollinsbury the tests at 23:01:02 and 23:02:30 failed, and the first answered test closed it.

recall.prompt: Which of these is a safe fallback when the real answer can't come?
options: A door that lets every fob in while the server is down
A dryer that runs and adds the charge to a known resident's monthly bill
A payment page that reports "paid" and never records the charge
A lift that ignores its safety checks until the server is back
recall.why: A fallback is safe when being wrong for a while is cheap and can be put right later. Pay later works because the residents are known and billed every month. Letting everyone in, losing the charge or skipping safety checks can't be put right afterwards.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The 2 payment helpers and pay later have worked all spring; Tillpenny hung twice more and nobody noticed but me. In May the lift company added a check-in: before a lift moves, the server asks the lift company's computer whether that lift is due a service, and waits up to 30 s. That call runs on the 8 shared helpers. On Tuesday evening their computer stopped answering. Between 18:10 and 18:13 the lifts stood still, and the front door refused 9 taps.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the front door fail again, and what should Juozas change?

keyIdeas.idea: The lift check waits on an outside computer from the same 8 helpers as the door, so its hang filled them and the fobs waited behind it
Every outside service needs its own small pool, not just payments: a bulkhead per service
A short timeout and a breaker on the lift check, with a safe fallback such as letting the lift run and recording the check for later

coldCase.model: It is the same shape as the dryers. The lift check calls an outside computer and waits up to 30 s, and it runs on the same 8 helpers as the door. When the lift company's computer hung, lift calls filled them, and the fobs waited behind the lift checks until the reader gave up. The fix last time fenced off payments only. Every outside service needs its own small pool, a bulkhead: say 2 helpers for the lift company, with no line, so its waiting can never reach the door's helpers. Give it a short timeout, a few seconds, and a breaker that fails fast while the company is down and tests with one call. Then pick a safe fallback: let the lift run as it did before May and record the check for later, since a missed service reminder can be caught up, and a lift that won't move is worse.
